# Matrix {#sec-matrixCoding}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Tableau matematika!
:::

A matrix is a machine language implementation of a matrix in mathematics @sec-matrixMath.
It is a rectangular object where each entry are identified by its row and column position.

Reusing the analogy of stacked apartment as a vector @sec-vector, the matrix allows multiple apartments in each floor. So an apartment is now identified by the floor number and the order in that floor. And similar to a vector, a matrix needs to be homogeneous.

In data science, data could be heterogeneous, in that case we could use data frame @sec-dataframe or @sec-list.
In general, a matrix object it is better used for mathematical computation.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
To construct a matrix, we need the informations: the size of the matrix: how many rows (nrow) and columns (ncol), the list of all the elements in a form of vectors so we need a vector of length nrow x ncol, and a way to indicate how to arrange the elements.

In R, to contruct a matrix we use matrix(), matrix_name <- matrix(data, nrow, ncol, byrow).
Most of the time, ncol is not because it is inferred from length of data divided by nrow.
byrow is argument that takes boolean telling whether it should be arranged by rows or by colums. The default is

See function @sec-functionCoding for

To access element, we use the same [] as in vector but with two dimensions [row position, column position].
Be aware that the first is vertical (as in floor number and the second is horizontal, and the order in that floor).

- matrix_name[1, 2] means to retrive the element in the first row (horizontal) and second column
- matrix_name[3, ] (leaving the second dimension empty) means taking the third row
- matrix[, 3] (leaving the first dimension empty) means taking the third column (see the output below)
- matrix [ -2 , -3] the negative means remove that specific column, or row, or both matrix []


## Examples {.unnumbered}

Use the matrix from @sec-matrix

- Construction
```{r}
#| echo: true
mat <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE)
mat
```

- Extraction of the first row, using index 1 while leaving the second dimension empty.

```{r}
mat[1]

mat[1, ]

```

- Extraction of the first column, using index 1 while leaving the first dimension empty.

```{r}
mat[, 1]

```

- Extraction of a specific element, for instance the element in the first row and third column
-
```{r}

mat[1, 3]

```

- Extraction of more than one element
```{r}
mat[1, c(1, 3)]

mat[c(1, 2), ]

mat[, c(1, 3)]

```

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- matrix is used in more mathematical way, mathematical operation @sec-matrix_op and @sec-matrix_multi. It is customary to just use index integer to extract elements
- We can also give a column name and row name to the data. However, it is not the most common way to use a matrix. It is more common to use data frame @sec-dataframe for that.
- Coercion work here too, because it has to be homogenous, boolean < integer < numeric < character
- Extract dimension with `dim()`
- There are things that can be done with transpose
-  Notice that there is no chapter on vector in basic mathematics, that is because, mathematically, a vector is simply a "one dimensional" matrix.
